title: Photography direction for a consumer brand
excerpt: Photograph the object so a stranger can name it. Refuse lead images that are only mood. The picture is part of the argument, and the phone will crop it.
alt: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk. A scene you can identify at a glance, which is the standard for a product photograph.
caption: A wide city avenue with yellow taxis, tall buildings, and people on the sidewalk. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a catalog photograph include?
faqs.answer: The object, large enough to name, on a repeatable ground, with the detail that carries the claim: the handle, the closure, the sole, the refill seating. Lifestyle can follow if the product stays the subject. A crop that turns the claim into texture is a weaker offer.

faqs.question: How many pictures does a product need?
faqs.answer: A clear catalog frame, one detail, and one use if use is not obvious. Repeat the ground and the light. A campaign frame is optional and should expire with the season. Two hundred near-duplicates are a delay, not a direction.

faqs.question: What should alt text say?
faqs.answer: Describe the object, the angle, and the ground. The W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines treat text alternatives as part of making content perceivable. A line about a ritual fails anyone who cannot see the picture, and it fails the shopper who needed the fact.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?

markdown:
Consumer brand website photography should show the object clearly. Refuse a manifesto that arrives before the product, including a manifesto made of pictures. The frames are part of the argument. A mood pasted under the headline is decoration, and a shopper who does not know you yet cannot buy decoration.

A stranger should be able to name the thing and imagine it in their hand or on their body. If the frame cannot do that, it is the wrong frame.

## The object has to be legible

Choose photographs where the product is large enough to name, on a ground that does not compete, with the working parts visible. The handle of the mug. The closure of the jacket. The cap of the bottle. The sole you claim is replaceable. Those details are the offer. A crop that turns them into texture is a different, weaker offer.

Lifestyle can come second. A hand holding the mug, at a scale where the mug is still the subject. A person walking in the jacket, with the cut visible from the side, not a face in a field of color where the garment is a smear. Context explains use. It should not erase the thing being used.

Nielsen Norman Group's article on [how long people stay](https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-long-do-users-stay-on-web-pages/) puts the first 10 seconds at the center of whether people stay. On a brand homepage those seconds are mostly picture. If the picture is mist, linen, and a slogan, the shopper learns your taste and not your product. Taste may be real. It is not a substitute for the object. Show the object while you still have their attention. People read only about a quarter of the words. They will see the picture.

Wabisabi, a public Hanabi brand site, is a reference for calm frames: the object allowed to be quiet and still specific. Down the Cove is the public shop example, an ecommerce migration and redesign where the goods had to remain recognizable. Borrow the standard. A picture direction is how you keep it after the first shoot, when someone adds a pretty file that does not show the product.

## One brief you can hand to anyone with the camera

Write the direction on a single page. Subject: the object, named, plus one use if use is not obvious. Crop: the product fills enough of the frame to identify, edges included when the silhouette matters. Ground: one background for the catalog, stated as a color and a material. Light: the light you can repeat in the studio or by a window, not a one-off sunset. Angle: front, three-quarter, and the detail that carries the claim.

Write the refusals beside it. No lead image where the product is unrecognizable. No stock scene of a life you do not sell. No filter that changes the color of the cloth, because the color is a fact. No text baked into the photograph. No trophy of a collaboration that hides the object you need the shopper to understand. No manifesto typeset across the only clear view of the product.

Use one crop for the catalog grid so the set feels like one brand. Mixing a square, a cinematic banner, and a portrait with different shadows makes even a good range look unfinished. The grid is a wall in the shop. The wall needs a rule.

Color accuracy is part of the brief. Photograph the object so the glaze, the dye, and the metal match what will arrive, under the light you named. If a glaze varies, show two true examples and say so in the caption. A single heroic sample that you cannot repeat is a promise. Captions can tell the truth in a few words. "Glaze pools at the rim; yours will vary." That line belongs next to the picture, not in a policy footer.

## The manifesto, when it tries to be a photograph

A manifesto-before-the-product often shows up as an image. Fog. An empty chair. A pair of anonymous hands pouring coffee with the mug cropped out. A sentence about slowness set in large type on a full-bleed photograph of a landscape. These frames reassure the team that the brand has a soul. The shopper still cannot buy.

If the landscape is truly part of the product, because you sell a record of that place or the material comes from it and the fact changes the purchase, use one frame, late, with a caption that states the fact. Do not open on it. Open on the object. The belief becomes visible when the thing supports it. In the other order, the picture demands agreement before the shopper knows what you sell.

Campaign images can exist. Give them a season and a shelf. The catalog images stay stable underneath, so a shopper who clicks through the campaign still lands on a clear product. When the season ends, retire the campaign frame. A homepage that still leads with last winter's fog is a manifesto that forgot its dates.

People in the pictures need a reason. A model wearing the jacket to show the cut is a reason. A model in a scene that never reveals the clothes is a casting exercise. Credit the practical goal in the brief so the next shoot does not drift back into pure mood. Hanabi's design work starts from that kind of brief. The pictures have a job. The job is the object.

## Details, sets, and the frame you owe the claim

If you claim a replaceable sole, photograph the sole and the method of replacement. If you claim a refill, photograph the refill fitting the bottle, including the moment of seating, not only the bottle in a beautiful room. If you sell a set, photograph the pieces both together and apart so the count is visible. The claim and the frame should match. A claim without a frame reads as copy. A frame without the claim's detail reads as lifestyle.

Scale helps. A hand, a table edge, a door, used carefully, tells the shopper whether the object is small. Avoid a scale that flatters. A tiny product shot on a huge seamless sweep can make a modest object look like a monument, and the unboxing will feel like a correction. Corrections at unboxing become returns.

Packaging is part of the product only if it changes the decision, such as a gift pouch you actually include. Photograph the pouch if it is included. Leave it out of the hero if it is optional and the picture would confuse what arrives. The hero is what a typical order contains.

Alt text, which you will write even though it is invisible, should describe the object in the frame. The W3C's [Web Content Accessibility Guidelines](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) treat text alternatives as part of making content perceivable. "Coast mug, stoneware, three-quarter view on a gray ground" is alt text. "Elevated morning ritual" is the manifesto again, and it fails anyone who cannot see the picture. Write the alt when you upload the file, while the brief is in your hand.

## A small set, repeated

You need fewer pictures than a moodboard suggests. For each product: the clear catalog frame, one detail that proves the claim, one use if use is non-obvious. Repeat the ground and the light. Add a campaign frame only when you have a season to attach it to. A folder of two hundred near-duplicates is not a direction. It is a delay.

Store the brief where the next person will find it. If files live in a shared place after the site launches, pin the direction there. Hanabi's client portal holds brand files and notes after delivery so the rule survives the end of the project. The rule is what keeps next March's pictures in the same family as this March's.

Replace a weak hero rather than covering it with type. A headline across a confusing crop confesses that the crop failed. Change the picture. Let the type name the product and state the one plain fact. Type should not have to explain what the pixels hid.

Build a contact sheet of the approved frames and pin it where uploads happen. Three frames per product is a full set: the catalog view, the detail that proves the claim, and one use if use is unclear. Anything else is optional and should be marked optional. When a new shoot arrives, compare it to the sheet before it touches the homepage. If the ground, the crop, or the color has drifted, correct the file or leave it in the archive. The archive can be large. The homepage cannot.

Write the alt text in the same pass, while you can still see the file. Name the object, the angle, and the ground. The shopper who cannot see the picture should receive the same fact the picture was hired to deliver.

## The phone will judge the crop

Most shoppers will meet the picture on a phone, in a tall crop, with the name and the path to the product competing for the width. Check every lead image at that size. A wide landscape often becomes a strip of sky. The object falls out of the frame. The argument falls with it.

That phone pass is the whole visit for many people. It is the subject of [the mobile visit for a consumer brand](/blog/the-mobile-visit-for-a-consumer-brand).

If you want to settle a photo brief before the next shoot, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the three frames you would trust on the homepage, and one you already know is only mood.
